results.title: What does it mean to be memory-bound? | GPU Glossary
results.content: NVIDIA CUDA Profiling Tools Interface. let us know on GitHub. # What does it mean to be memory-bound? Kernels that are memory-bound are limited by the memory bandwidth of the GPU. Specifically, they are limited by the bandwidth between the GPU RAM and the local cache of the Streaming Multiprocessors , because the problems of interest for GPU performance generally have working set sizes much larger than any higher level of the memory hierarchy . Memory-bound kernels have a lower arithmetic intensity (fewer operations per byte moved), relative to the ridge point of their roofline model . Technically, memory-boundedness is only defined for a single kernel , as part of the roofline model , but with a bit of squinting it can be generalized to cover the multiple kernels that make up a typical workload. Contemporary large language model inference workloads are often memory-bound during the decode/output generation stage, when the weights must be loaded once in each forward pass. That happens once per output token, unless multi-token prediction or speculative decoding are used, which makes it easy to calculate the minimum latency between tokens (intertoken latency or time per output token) for memory-bound Transformer large language model inference. Assume the model has 500B parameters, stored in 16-bit precision, for a total of 1 TB. If we run inference on a single GPU with a memory bandwidth of 10 TB/s, we can load the weights once every 100 ms, and that puts a lower bound on our intertoken latency. By batching multiple inputs together, we can linearly increase the number of floating point operations done per parameter loaded (the arithmetic intensity ), in principle up to the point of compute-boundedness , without incurring any additional latency, which implies that the throughput improves linearly in the batch size. results.content: What are the common memory access patterns used in large language model training? All content displayed below is AI generate content. Some content may not be accurate. What are the common memory access patterns used in large language model training? Training large language models (LLMs) involves complex memory access patterns due to the massive scale of computations and data movement. Efficient memory utilization is critical for performance, especially when working with high-performance GPUs like the NVIDIA A100, H100, or L40S. Below are the most common memory access patterns observed in LLM training workflows. ### Sequential Access for Input Data During the forward and backward passes, LLMs process input sequences in a mostly sequential manner. * Token embeddings being loaded in batches from GPU memory. * Layer activations being computed and stored in a predictable, step-by-step fashion. * Attention mechanisms accessing key-value pairs in a structured sequence. ### Random Access for Attention Mechanisms Transformer-based models heavily rely on self-attention, which introduces semi-random memory access patterns: * Query-key-value matrices require scattered reads and writes across different memory locations. * Softmax operations access probability distributions in a non-linear fashion. * Multi-head attention splits computations across different memory regions. ### Strided Memory Access for Matrix Operations Matrix multiplications (GEMM operations) dominate LLM training and use strided patterns: * Weight matrices are accessed in large, contiguous blocks with regular strides. ### Memory-Bound Operations in Optimization Optimizers like Adam or SGD introduce additional memory access challenges: * First and second moment estimates require frequent updates to small memory regions. * Mixed-precision training alternates between FP16 and FP32 memory accesses. * Gradient accumulation loops increase memory pressure with larger batch sizes. ### Memory Hierarchy Utilization Modern GPUs leverage multiple memory hierarchies to accelerate LLM training: HBM (High Bandwidth Memory)Stores model parameters and large activations L2 Cache Caches frequently accessed weight matrices Shared Memory Used for attention score computations Registers Hold intermediate values during kernel execution Understanding these memory access patterns helps optimize LLM training on NVIDIA data center GPUs. The A100 and H100 series, with their large memory capacities and advanced caching mechanisms, are particularly well-suited to handle these demanding workloads efficiently. ### Need GPU Compute?

results.title: CCA: Cost-Capacity-Aware Caching for In-Memory Data Analytics Frameworks
results.content: # CCA: Cost-Capacity-Aware Caching for In-Memory Data Analytics Frameworks. In this paper, we propose an application-specific cost-capacity-aware caching scheme for in-memory data analytics frameworks. We use a cost model, built from multiple representative inputs, and an execution flow analysis, extracted from DAG schedule, to select primary candidates to cache among intermediate data. As most data analytics frameworks operate with the directed acyclic graph (DAG), which is the lineage information of the data processing, deciding which data to cache from the execution flow specified in the DAG is an appropriate approach but still not trivial [6,7]. In this paper, we propose a cost-capacity-aware caching (CCA) for in-memory data analytics frameworks. CCA makes caching decisions to maximize the predicted performance benefit based on the computing cost model. In addition to computing cost, caching decision in CCA depends on execution contexts, such as cache capacity, input data size, and execution stage progress. In addition to data reuse times, for optimal performance, it is necessary to compare execution cost through recomputing for recovery and performance gain due to caching. In-memory analytics frameworks store intermediate data in the cache memory to improve the performance of iterative operations. In addition, in big data processing, operator’s cost and cache capacity are important metrics to obtain optimal performance. Least cost strategy (LCS) [16] is a cost-aware eviction policy for efficiently managing cache memory instead of the default LRU policy in the data analytics frameworks. Many other studies have argued that the execution flow should be considered in an in-memory big data processing framework where caching is important. As we compared our CCA and LCS in Section 5.5, CCA directly and automatically determined the caching decision to optimize the execution flow and showed near-optimal performance no matter what the memory situation. results.title: Mind the Memory Gap: Unveiling GPU Bottlenecks in Large-Batch LLM Inference for CLOUD 2025 - IBM Research
results.content: # Mind the Memory Gap: Unveiling GPU Bottlenecks in Large-Batch LLM Inference. Large language models have been widely adopted across different tasks, but their auto-regressive generation nature often leads to inefficient resource utilization during inference. While batching is commonly used to increase throughput, per-formance gains plateau beyond a certain batch size, especially with smaller models, a phenomenon that existing literature typically explains as a shift to the compute-bound regime. In this paper, through an in-depth GPU-level analysis, we reveal that large-batch inference remains memory-bound, with most GPU compute capabilities underutilized due to DRAM bandwidth saturation as the primary bottleneck. The freed memory and underutilized GPU compute capabilities can then be leveraged by concurrent workloads. Specifically, we use model replication to improve serving throughput and GPU utilization. Our findings challenge conventional assumptions about LLM inference, offering new in-sights and practical strategies for improving resource utilization, particularly for smaller language models. Nikoleta Iliakopoulou, Jovan Stojkovic, et al. Haoran Qiu, Weichao Mao, et al.
